analysis.one_liner: Lets investors sue people who knowingly or recklessly help someone commit securities fraud.
analysis.headline: The bill, co-sponsored by the House Financial Services chairman, was sent to a subcommittee in July 2010 and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Since a 1994 Supreme Court decision, private investors can only sue the main wrongdoer in a securities fraud — not the banks, advisers, or others who knowingly helped carry it out. This bill would change that, letting defrauded investors bring civil suits against anyone who knowingly or recklessly provides substantial help to a violation of the securities laws, with liability equal to the main violator's. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who lose money to securities fraud. They would gain a way to recover damages not just from the primary violator, but from the banks, broker-dealers, advisers, and others who knowingly or recklessly helped the fraud happen — which also raises the cost of participating in fraud and could deter it.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a private right of action to Section 20(e) of the Securities Exchange Act against any person who knowingly or recklessly provides substantial assistance to a violation of the securities laws.
Makes the aider and abettor liable 'to the same extent as' the primary violator, so investors could reach deep-pocketed secondary actors, not just the initial wrongdoer.
Also extends the aiding-and-abetting standard for SEC enforcement actions to include recklessness, not just knowing conduct.
Had 10 House sponsors and cosponsors, all Democrats, including Barney Frank, the chairman of the Financial Services Committee to which the bill was referred.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, broker-dealers, investment firms, and professional advisers such as auditors and lawyers, who would face new civil lawsuits from private investors alleging they substantially assisted a securities violation — with liability as large as the primary violator's. Some litigation costs would ultimately be passed to investors and customers through higher fees.

drawbacks.text: The standard is broad: it covers 'recklessly' as well as knowingly providing 'substantial assistance,' with no statutory limits on what counts as substantial assistance or on who can be sued, which invites litigation against secondary and peripheral actors rather than only the true wrongdoers.

Liable parties are on the hook 'to the same extent as' the primary violator, meaning a peripheral helper could face the same damages bill as the fraudster, a cost that financial firms argue raises the price of ordinary business for their customers.

Broader private litigation against banks and advisers also raises defense and settlement costs across the financial sector, some share of which gets passed through to ordinary investors in fees and spreads.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and aimed at ordinary investors: after the Supreme Court's 1994 Central Bank decision, private plaintiffs could no longer sue enablers of securities fraud at all, leaving recovery against knowing helpers to SEC enforcement alone. The bill's main design weakness is that its standard is deliberately sweeping — recklessness plus unlimited 'substantial assistance' plus full primary-level liability — which invited the objection that routine bankers, auditors, and lawyers could be dragged into suits alongside actual fraudsters. A narrower version could have targeted knowing enablers while limiting peripheral exposure; as written, the deterrence benefit and the over-litigation risk were both real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2010, referred to two committees, then sent to a Judiciary subcommittee in July, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2011 without ever getting a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the bill on April 15, 2010, joined by Rep. Barney Frank, chairman of the House Financial Services Committee.
It was referred to both the Financial Services and Judiciary Committees on the day of introduction.
On July 26, 2010, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts and Competition Policy, the last action ever taken on it.
Neither committee held a markup, no vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died at the end of the 111th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, broker-dealers, and professional advisers came out ahead: they avoided a new source of private lawsuits from investors, and defrauded investors were left with only the main violator to sue.

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create private aiding-and-abetting liability for securities violations.

against.name: House Financial Services and Judiciary Committees
against.role: Committees of referral in the 111th House
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral; the bill was sent to the Subcommittee on Courts and Competition Policy in July 2010 and never marked up or reported.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all 10 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on, so any party split on the merits was never tested on the record.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed them to private investor lawsuits whenever they knowingly or recklessly substantially assisted a securities violation, with liability equal to the primary violator's. It died, so that exposure never materialized.

industries.industry: Auditors, law firms, and other professional advisers
industries.note: These secondary actors were the classic targets of aiding-and-abetting claims before the 1994 Supreme Court ruling; the bill would have restored that private liability. Its death kept them off the hook.
A private right of action against aiders and abettors would have created a large pool of new defendants and claims for investor-side lawyers. It never became law.
